This has taught me to think beyond a schematic and consider how hardware is assembled, inspected, maintained and prepared for real-world use.

I also explore Claude with MCP integrations as an AI-assisted engineering workflow for supporting design tasks. I describe these as developing skills rather than claiming commercial PCB-design experience.

How I approach hardware

From engineering concept to physical product

The combination I would bring to a junior embedded-hardware team: electronics fundamentals, project-based embedded prototyping and practical experience in a production environment.

01 · Understand the circuit

Start from system requirements, sensor signals, component functions and datasheets. My BCI project connected EEG acquisition and signal classification with an Arduino-controlled hardware platform.

02 · Prototype and integrate

Build around microcontrollers, sensors, motor drivers and communication modules. My academic prototypes used Arduino, Bluetooth, ultrasonic sensing and simulated circuits in Tinkercad.

03 · Build for production

At Meyn, work with drawings, physical components, assembly procedures, fit and alignment checks, and quality workflows. I understand why design decisions must translate into hardware that can be assembled and inspected.

Current development focus: EasyEDA and KiCad schematic capture, component selection and PCB layout. Oscilloscope, logic-analyser, SMD rework, DRC sign-off and physical prototype validation are not claimed unless separately demonstrated.

Embedded systems project: EEG-controlled wheelchair

BSc thesis: an embedded prototype that translated SSVEP brain-signal selections into movement commands for a low-cost wheelchair platform. The project combined signal processing, Arduino control, wireless communication, motor drivers and obstacle sensing.

  • Data: two subjects, four visual stimuli (9, 10, 12 and 15 Hz), eight EEG channels.
  • Signal processing: band-pass filter, then CCA feature classification giving two correlation coefficients, then a threshold decision to produce a command.
  • Control: commands sent over Bluetooth (HC-06) to an Arduino and motor drivers: forward, backward, left, right, stop.
  • Safety: ultrasonic sensor for obstacle detection.
  • Hardware: small-scale prototype on an acrylic chassis with Arduino Uno, DC motors, motor drivers, Bluetooth module, ultrasonic sensor and battery. Circuit designed and simulated in Tinkercad.

Selected hardware & prototyping projects

The projects below combine completed academic prototypes with current PCB design studies. Each project is labelled by its actual stage; proposed hardware is not presented as fabricated or bench-verified.

Obstacle-avoiding wheelchair

Four DC motors driven through two L293D H-bridges, commanded over serial (forward, back, left, right, stop). An ultrasonic sensor halts the motors when an obstacle is closer than 90 cm, with direction LEDs and a pushbutton stop.

Arduino CL293DUltrasonicTinkercad

LCD digital thermometer

A TMP36 sensor read on the ADC, converted from voltage to °C and °F, and shown on a 16×2 LCD every second.

TMP36ADCLiquidCrystalTinkercad

Heart-rate detector

A 4th-order IIR filter, with coefficients designed in MATLAB, implemented in Arduino C. Threshold peak detection gives beats per minute averaged over three beats, with RGB LED output. Tested with a signal source, oscilloscope and multimeter in simulation.

MATLABIIR filterSignal processingTinkercad

Featured assistive technology project

Advanced blind stick

A connected mobility-aid concept combining obstacle and water detection with location sharing and alerts for a caregiver.

Project poster · Design and Implementation of Advanced Blind Stick Using GPS and GSM Module

Project overview

More awareness. More independence.

The project explores an assistive walking stick that can detect nearby obstacles and water, provide feedback to the user, and share an emergency alert with a caretaker.

01

Obstacle detection

Ultrasonic sensors are positioned at different heights to detect objects along the user's path.

02

Water detection

A water sensor is placed near the bottom of the stick to help identify water in front of the user.

03

Feedback and alerts

A vibration motor and buzzer provide local feedback. The concept also describes sending distance and location information to a caretaker in an emergency.

04

Embedded system

The presentation describes GPS and GSM modules, Bluetooth, a Raspberry Pi and a PIC18F4525 microcontroller as part of the system design.

Biomedical engineering·Project breakdown

Designing an advanced blind stick: connecting sensing, feedback and location awareness

A walking stick can do more than provide physical support. By combining sensors, embedded control and communication modules, it can become an assistive device that helps users understand their surroundings and contact someone when they need support.

Start with the user's environment

The first design challenge is detecting hazards that a conventional stick may not identify early enough. In this project, ultrasonic sensors are placed at two different heights. The presentation specifies positions of approximately 17 cm and 92 cm from the bottom of the stick. A separate water sensor is positioned near the tip to detect water on the path.

Turn sensor readings into useful feedback

Detection is only useful when the information reaches the person in a clear way. The design includes a vibration motor near the handgrip and a buzzer. These outputs offer two ways to communicate a warning without relying only on a visual display.

Add communication for emergency situations

The project also describes GPS and GSM functionality. In an emergency — for example, when a hazard such as fire or water is detected — the system is intended to send an alert with location and distance information to a caretaker's phone. Bluetooth is included in the presented system architecture as another communication link.

Think about the complete embedded system

The presentation describes a PVC stick structure and lists components including a GPS module, Raspberry Pi, PIC18F4525 microcontroller, ultrasonic sensors, water sensor, vibration motor, buzzer and power bank. These parts need to work as one system: sensing, processing, user feedback, power and communication all influence reliability and usability.

What matters beyond the prototype?

For an assistive device, a successful demonstration is only one step. A real-world version would need careful testing of detection range, false alarms, battery life, weather resistance, communication coverage, physical comfort and fail-safe behaviour. The user should also be able to understand alerts quickly and use the device without unnecessary complexity.

This project reflects what I find interesting about biomedical engineering: bringing hardware, software and human needs together to solve a practical problem.
